pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the name ​is ​**/bɛs/ ​(conventional)** ​— ‌Conventional ​reading ​— ‌Egyptian ​vocalisation not ‌attested.[^1]

​Phoneme ‌by ​phoneme:

- ​**Bs** ​— ​Written ​bs; ‌conventionally vocalised ​“Bes”. ‌The ​name ‌is ​of ‌uncertain ​etymology ‌— ​perhaps Nubian ​in ‌origin.
- ‌**** ‌— ​The ​dwarf-god ‌of ​hearth, ​childbirth, and ‌the ​protection ​of ‌the ​vulnerable.

‌For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ‌is: ​“BESS”

‌Kindred ​and ​historical ‌forms of ‌the ‌name:

- ‌**Greek** ​— ‌Βῆς ​(Bês); ​associated ​in ‌late periods ​with ​the ​Pataikoi

‌A ​god ​whose ​image ‌was ​more famous ‌than ​his ‌name ​— ‌everyone ‌knew ​the ​dwarf, ​few could ​say ‌who ‌he ​was.

sources.citation: Deir el-Medina birth and Bes-chamber scenes.

domains.body:
**Bs** ​— Bes ‌— ‌is Egypt’s ​household ​god: ​the dwarf ​with ​the lion’s ‌mane ​and the ​fright-mask ‌face who ​stands ‌at ​the head ‌of ​the bed, ​the ​birth-brick, the ​mirror-handle ​and the ‌harp, ​keeping ‌every dangerous ​thing ‌away from ​the ‌vulnerable. No ​temple ‌was his; ​every ​home ‌was. He ‌is ‌the most ​reproduced ​and least ‌narrated ​god of ​Egypt.[^1]

### ‌Guardian ​of the ​Hearth

‌His image ​watched ‌over beds, ​births, ​and ​mirrors — ​the ‌god of ‌the ​domestic threshold.

### ‌The ​Dancer-Demon

His ​terrifying ‌face ‌and acrobatic ‌dance ‌frighten away ​the ‌demons of ​childbirth ​and sleep.

### ​Lord ‌of ​Childbirth

The ​birth-brick ​and the ‌Bes-mask ​of the ​midwife: ​he presided ‌over ​every ‌Egyptian child’s ​first ‌hour.

### Protector ​of ‌Sleep

Bes-guardians ‌on ​headrests and ​bed-legs ​watched ​the sleeper ‌through ‌the dangerous ​night.

mythology.body:
Bes has ​no myth because ‌he was always ‌already there — ​at the door, ​at the bed, ​at the birth. His ​‘theology’ is apotropaic: ​power through ugliness, ‌protection through fright. ​Later tradition gave ​him a birth ‌and a family ​(the lion-dwarf Pantheos ‌of the late ​period), but his ‌real domain never ​moved from the threshold ​of ordinary Egyptian ​life.[^1]

### The Mask ​of the Midwife ​(Birth Protection)

In ‌the birth-chamber, the ​midwife donned the ‌Bes-mask and danced ​his dance; his ‌grimace drew the ​malign spirits’ attention ‌onto himself and away ​from mother and ‌child. The *Beset*-amulets ​and the ‘Bes-chamber’ ​scenes of Deir ‌el-Medina show the ‌rite in domestic ‌detail.[^2]

### The Dwarf ​Who Amuses the ​Gods (Papyrus Westcar ‌Analogy)

The Westcar ​Papyrus’ wonder-tale of the ​dwarf Dedi, who ‌dances and performs ​before the court, ​is read as ‌Bes’ narrative shadow ​— the small ‌deformed being whose ​skill and humour ​carry more power ​than the great. ​Bes never speaks in ‌the texts; he ‌dances.

### Bes the ​Pantheos (Late Period ‌Theology)

By the ​Late Period, Bes ​absorbed attributes of ‌every major god ‌— the wings ‌of Horus, the ‌crown of Amun, ​the snakes of Mehen ‌— becoming the ​‘Pantheos-Bes’, one dwarf ​wearing the whole ​pantheon’s power. The ‌type, with its ​many arms and ​animal faces, spread ​through the Greco-Roman ‌world as an ​amulet-image.

### The Son ​of the Great Goddess ​(Tutu & Bes)

‌At Saqqara and ​in the demotic ‌tales, Bes appears ​as the son ‌of Neith, sent ​against the enemies ‌of the gods ‌— a dwarf-hero ​with a sword. ​The strand gives him ​a genealogy the ​earlier household cult ‌never needed: the ‌protector domesticated into ​a champion.

overview.body:
**Bs** ​(*bes*) — ‌The Protector ‌of ​Hearth and ​Childbirth · ​The ​protector — ​belongs to ‌the ​Egyptian tradition, ​where it ‌is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Protection, ‌Childbirth, Joy". ​The name ​means ​"The protector"[^1].

​**Bs** — ​Bes ‌— is ​Egypt’s household ‌god: ​the dwarf ‌with the ​lion’s ‌mane and ​the fright-mask ‌face ​who stands ​at the ‌head ‌of the ‌bed, the ​birth-brick, ​the mirror-handle ‌and the ​harp, ​keeping every ‌dangerous thing ​away ​from the ‌vulnerable. No ​temple was ‌his; ​every home ​was. He ​is ​the most ‌reproduced and ‌least ​narrated god ‌of Egypt.[^2]

​PuniCodex ​records the ‌canonical scholarly ‌spelling ‌**Bs** and ‌serves its ​temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/bes/). The ​displayed ​form is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ‌form *bes* ​contains the ‌same ​letters: no ‌recovered diacritics ​or ‌special encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested ​in Hieroglyphs ​as ​**𓃀𓋴𓄜**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means ​"The ​protector"[^1].

‌The ​canonical spelling ‌**Bs** ​matches ‌the ​conventional ​scholarly ​romanization. ​The ​plain ‌ASCII form ​*bes* ‌contains ​the ‌same ​letters, ‌so ​no ‌lost ​diacritics or ​encoding ‌transition ‌is ‌claimed. ​The ​editorial ‌work ​is ​to fix ‌one ​reviewed ​reference ‌spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and ​provenance, and ​keep ​the ‌original ‌evidence ​visible. ‌The ​displayed ​form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ‌a ‌description ​computed ‌from ​the ​displayed ​form ‌itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**b** ​→ ​**B** ​— ‌Same, ​capitalized
- **e** ‌→ ​**s** ‌— ​Special ‌phonetic ‌character
- ​**s** ​→ ​**—** — ​Dropped: ‌vowel ‌not ​written
